(p-264) Surah "Al-Zukhruf" (The Adornment)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ He swore by the Book that makes things clear, which is the Qur'an, and made His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, We have made it﴾, meaning: We made it (ṣayyarnāhu, "We rendered it" or "We brought it into being").

﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, the answer to the oath (jawāb al-qasam). This is one of the fine and innovative (badī'ah) forms of oath, owing to the harmony (tanāsub) between the oath and what is sworn to.

As for "al-mubīn" (the clear one): it means the one that makes things clear (al-bayyin) to those to whom it was revealed, because it is in their language and their modes of expression (asālībihim). Or it means the one that is evident (al-wāḍiḥ) to those who reflect (al-mutadabbirīn). Or it means the one that has made clear the paths of guidance from the paths of misguidance, and has made clear everything the community needs in matters of religious practice (abwāb al-diyānah).

﴿so that you may understand﴾, meaning: so that you may comprehend its meanings (ma'ānīhi).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 4:

﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us﴾, and the Qur'an is recorded with Allah in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Its proof is His saying: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ [al-Buruj: 21] ﴿in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 22]. It is called "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book) because it is the origin in which the books were recorded, from which they are transmitted and copied. "Inni al-Kitab" (with a kasra on the alif), is the reading of ʿAli and Hamzah.

﴿La-ʿAliyyun﴾: two predicates, meaning: at the highest levels of eloquence; or, exalted in rank among the books, because it is miraculous among them.

﴿Hakimun﴾: possessing far-reaching wisdom.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 5:

﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you﴾, (meaning:) shall We then remove the Reminder from you and push it away from you?! (p-265) It is used metaphorically, from their saying: "He drove the strange camels away from the watering-trough" (ḍaraba al-gharā'ib ʿan al-ḥawḍ). The fa' (then) is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon an omitted element whose estimated sense is: "Shall We leave you alone, and then turn away the Reminder from you?!" It is a rejection (inkār) of the matter being contrary to what was previously set forth: His sending down the Book, and making it an Arabic Qur'an so that you might understand it and act upon its obligations.

﴿ṣafḥan﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from "ṣafaḥa ʿanhu", meaning he turned away from him, and it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), with the meaning: "Shall We withhold from you the sending down of the Qur'an and the establishing of the proof through it, turning away from you?!" It is also permissible for it to be a verbal noun of a different form (ʿalā khilāf al-maṣdar), since it is said: "ḍarabtu ʿanhu", meaning I turned away from him. So said al-Farrā'.

﴿in kuntum﴾ — with the reading of "in" (if) as "li-an" (because) and "kuntum" — "in kuntum" is the reading of Madani and Hamza. It belongs to the type of conditional that proceeds from one who is confident of the soundness of the matter, the fulfilment of which is certain, as a hired worker says: "If I have worked for you, then pay me my due," while he knows that this is so.

﴿qawman musrifīn﴾ — excessive (mufrițīn) in ignorance, exceeding the limit in misguidance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 6:

﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples﴾ — that is: We sent many messengers to those who came before you.

"And no prophet comes to them except that they used to mock him." This is a narration of a past, continuing state: that is, they were persisting in this. And this is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the mockery of his people.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 8:

﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾: "stronger than them in might" (ashadda minhum batshan) is a specification (tamyiz), and the pronoun refers to "those who were extravagant" (al-musrifin), because He turned the address away from them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), informing him about them.

﴿And the example of the former peoples has passed on﴾: that is, their account has preceded in the Qur'an, in more than one place in it, the mention of their story and their wondrous condition, which is fitting that it should travel as a proverb (mathal). This is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a warning to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 9:

﴿And if you asked them﴾, i.e., the polytheists,

﴿"Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 10:

﴿Who has made the earth for you a cradle,﴾ "Kufi" reading: meaning a place of settling (qarar). Others read it "mihadan," meaning places of settling.

﴿and has made for you therein roads,﴾ meaning paths,

﴿that you may be guided.﴾ That is, so that you may find your way in your journeys.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 11:

﴿And He who sends down water from the sky in a measure﴾, in a quantity by which the servants are kept safe and the lands are in need of it,

﴿so We revive thereby a dead land﴾, that is, We give it life. This is a shift (ʿudūl) from the third person (al-mughāyabah) to the first person plural (al-ikhbār), because the addressee already knows the intended meaning. "Yazīd" reads "mayyitan" (with a shadda).

﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾, from your graves, alive. "Tukhrajūn" (with the verb in the passive, as "tukhrajūna") is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. There is no pause at "al-ʿAlīm," because "alladhī" is its attribute (ṣifah). Abū Ḥātim did pause there, on the assumption of the implied "Huwa alladhī" (He is the One who). These descriptions are not part of the speech of the disbelievers, because they deny being brought forth from the graves, so how would they say, "Thus you will be brought forth"? Rather, the verse is a proof against them in their denial of the resurrection.

﴿And He who created all the pairs, the kinds,⁠﴾

﴿all of them, and made for you ships and cattle, that you ride⁠﴾: i.e., that you ride upon. It is said, "they rode in the ships" (رَكِبُوا في الفُلْكِ) and "they rode the cattle" (رَكِبُوا الأنْعامَ). The transitive form without an intermediary (المُتَعَدِّي بِغَيْرِ واسِطَةٍ) took precedence over the form with an intermediary (المُتَعَدِّي بِواسِطَةٍ) because of its strength, so it was said: "تَرْكَبُونَهُ" (you ride it).

To stand firmly upon its back: on the backs of what you ride, namely the ship and the livestock,

﴿then remember﴾ with your hearts ﴿the favour of your Lord when you are settled upon them, and say﴾ with your tongues,

﴿"Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us"﴾, that is, made this mount tame,

﴿"and we could not have overpowered it"﴾, that is, been capable of it. It is said: "aqrana al-shay'" (he made the thing submit to him) when he was able to manage it. The literal meaning of "aqrana-hu" is that he found it to be his equal (qarina), because the difficult thing cannot be a companion (qarina) to the weak.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 14:

﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will surely return.﴾ (We will surely return to Him on the Day of Return.) It was said: they mention, when mounting the vehicles of this world, the last vehicle they ride from it, which is the bier (janazah). It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he placed his foot in the stirrup he would say: "In the name of Allah," and when he had settled upon the mount he would say: "Praise be to Allah for every condition,

﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it ourselves. And indeed, to our Lord we will surely return﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 13–14]" and he would say "Allahu akbar" three times and "La ilaha illa Allah" three times. And they said: when one boards a ship he should say: ﴿In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Hud: 41]. It is related that a group of people rode, and they said: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 13], to the end of the verse, and among them was a man on a she-camel that did not move due to its emaciation. He said: "I will certainly master this one," so it threw him off by its leaping, and his neck was broken. It is fitting that the intelligent rider does not ride for leisure and pleasure, but for reflection, and that he contemplates while doing so that he is surely perishing, and returning to Allah, not escaping His decree.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 15:

﴿And they have assigned to Him a portion from His servants.﴾ It is connected to His saying: "And if you were to ask them..." That is: "And if you were to ask them about the Creator of the heavens and the earth, they would surely acknowledge Him. Yet, despite that acknowledgment, they have assigned to Him a portion from His servants." That is, they said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Thus they made them a part of Him and a portion of Him, just as a child is a part of his father. "Juzu'an" (a part) is read as "juzu'" by Abu Bakr and Hammad.

﴿Indeed, man is clearly ungrateful.﴾ That is, he is manifestly denying the blessing, his denial being evident, because attributing a child to Him is disbelief, and disbelief is the root of all ingratitude.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 16:

﴿Has He taken for Himself daughters from what He creates, and has He favoured you with sons?﴾ That is: "Rather, has He taken [daughters]?" The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denial, for ignorance-exposure (tajhil) and for expressing astonishment at their condition, since they claimed that He chose for Himself the lesser rank, while they themselves have the higher one.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 17:

﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, [it is] by the kind which he has made to be a likeness for Him, i.e., a resemblance, because when he makes the angels a part of God and a portion of Him, he has made them of His kind and similar to Him, since a child can only be of the same kind as its parent.

﴿His face becomes darkened, and he is furious inwardly﴾, meaning that they attributed this kind to Him. And among their condition was that when one of them was told, "A daughter has been born to you," he became distressed, and his face turned dark out of rage and grief, and he was filled with (p-268) anguish. And "ẓalla" here carries the meaning of "ṣayrūrah" (becoming).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 18:

"Is one who is brought up in ornaments, and who, in disputation, is not clear [in expression]?" That is: "Is it that to the Most Merciful is ascribed as offspring one who bears this blameworthy attribute, namely that he is brought up in ornaments," i.e., "is nurtured" (yatarabba), "in adornment and luxury, and that when he needs to contend with opponents and vie with men, he is not clear, having no eloquence and bringing no proof? That is because of the weakness of their intellects." Muqatil said: "A woman does not speak except that she brings an argument against herself." In this is also the point that He made being raised in adornment one of the defects, so it is incumbent upon a man to avoid that and to adorn himself with the garment of piety. And "man" (man) is in the accusative position in terms of its grammatical place, and the meaning is: "Have they made the one who is brought up in ornaments - meaning daughters - to be for God, Mighty and Majestic?!"

"Yunashsha'" (is brought up) is read by Hamzah, 'Ali and Hafs, i.e., "is nurtured" (yurabba). They have combined in one act of disbelief three acts of disbelief, for they attributed offspring to God, attributed to Him the lowlier of the two kinds, and made them (the angels) from among the honoured angels, and so they belittled them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 19:

﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females.﴾ That is: they named them, and said that they are females. "With (ʿinda) the Most Merciful" — read by Makki, Madani and Shami (Ibn ʿAmir): the "ʿindiyyah" (nearness) is one of rank and status, not of place and location. "Al-ʿibad" is the plural of "ʿabd" (servant), and it is the more forceful term in argument with the obstinate, because of the contrast between servitude (ʿubudiyyah) and offspring (wilad).

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ This is a mockery of them, meaning: they say this without their saying being based on knowledge. God did not compel them to know this, nor did they reach it through any proof, nor did they comprehend it through a report that yields certain knowledge, nor did they witness their creation so as to report from direct observation.

﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾, the testimony they bore concerning the angels' femaleness,

﴿and they will be questioned﴾ about it. This is a threat.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 20:

﴿And they say, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them,"﴾ i.e., the angels. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that God does not will unbelief) clung to the apparent meaning of this verse, arguing that Allah (exalted is He) did not will unbelief from the unbeliever, and that He willed only faith. For the unbelievers claimed that Allah willed unbelief from them and did not will from them the abandonment of worshipping idols, since they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." That is, "Had He willed from us that we abandon the worship of idols, He would have prevented us from worshipping them, but He willed from us the worship of idols." Allah (exalted is He) rejected their statement and their belief with His words: ﴿They have no knowledge of that. They only guess.﴾ That is, they lie. The meaning of the verse, in our view, is that they intended by "willing" "approval," and they said: "Had He not approved of this, He would have hastened our punishment, or He would have prevented us from worshipping them by compulsion and constraint. Since He did not do that, He has approved of it." So Allah (exalted is He) rejected them with His words: "They have no knowledge of that," and so on. Or they said this statement in utter mockery and without belief, so Allah (exalted is He) refuted them in it and showed their ignorance, since they did not say it out of belief, as He said, reporting about them: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47]. This is true in principle, but when they said it mockingly, Allah refuted them with His words: ﴿You are only in clear error﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47]. Likewise Allah (exalted is He) said: ﴿They say, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], then said: ﴿And Allah testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], because they did not say it out of belief. They made the will (of Allah) a proof for themselves regarding what they did by their own choice, and they supposed that Allah would not punish them for anything they did by His will, and they regarded themselves as excused in that. So Allah (exalted is He) refuted them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 21:

﴿Or have We given them a Book before this (Qur'an), so that they are holding fast to it?﴾ That is, before the Qur'an, or before their present statement (that the angels are daughters of God).

﴿So they are holding fast to it﴾: that is, taking hold of it and acting upon it. It has also been said: there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and its implied sense is: "Did they witness their creation? Or have We given them a Book before it, in which it is stated that the angels are females?"

﴿Nay, they say﴾. Nay, they have no proof to cling to, neither from direct observation, nor from reason, nor from revelation (al-sam'), except their saying: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:23], that is, upon a religion, so we imitated them (taqlid). It derives from "al-umm," which means intention (al-qasd). So "al-ummah" is the path that is aimed at (tu'amm), that is, that is intended.

﴿And indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a complement (silah) to "muhtadun" (guided), or the two of them are predicates (khabar).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 23:

﴿And thus We did not send before you any warner into a town, except that its affluent ones said: "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ [The word "nabi" (prophet) is added here as an explanation of "nadhir" (warner).]

﴿Its affluent ones said﴾, i.e., (p-270) its people who lived in luxury (mutana''imuha), and they are those whom prosperity (al-ni'mah) made insolent (atraftahum), i.e., made them haughty (abtarathum). So they love nothing but desires and amusements, and they shun the hardships of the religion (mashaqqa al-din) and its obligations (takalifahu),

﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾. This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and a clarification that blind imitation of forefathers (taqlid al-aba') is an ancient disease.

﴿قالَ﴾ "Shāmiyy wa-Ḥafṣ" (read by al-Shāmī [Ibn ʿĀmir] and Ḥafṣ): that is, *al-nadhīr* (the warner) said it. "﴿قُلْ﴾" (*qul*, "Say!"), (read by) others, meaning: it was said to the warner, "Say!"

﴿قالَ أوَلَوْ جِئْتُكم بِأهْدى مِمّا وجَدْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ آباءَكُمْ﴾ meaning: "Will you follow your fathers even if I bring you a religion more rightly guided than the religion of your forefathers?!" ﴿قالُوا إنّا بِما أُرْسِلْتُمْ بِهِ كافِرُونَ﴾: "We are steadfast upon the religion of our fathers, and even if you bring us what is more rightly guided, and more rightly guided."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 25:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾: We punished them with what they deserved for their persistence (in disbelief),

﴿So observe how was the end of the deniers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 26:

﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father and his people﴾ i.e., remember when he said,

﴿"Indeed, I am free (barraʾ) from what you worship"﴾ i.e., barīʾ. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in which the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine and the feminine are alike, just as you say "rajulun ʿadlun" (a just man), "imraʾatun ʿadlun" (a just woman), and "qawmun ʿadlun" (a just people), and the meaning is "possessor of justice" (dhū ʿadl), "possessor of justice" (dhāt ʿadl),

﴿from what you worship﴾

(Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Surah 43, verse 27)

﴿Except He who created me, for He will guide me﴾. This is an exceptive (istithna') that is disjunct (munqati'), as if he had said: "But He who created me [is the one I worship]." ﴿Then surely He will guide me﴾: He will keep me firm upon guidance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 28:

﴿And He made it﴾: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) made the word of tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness), which he spoke, a lasting word. It was his statement: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 26-27], ﴿a word that remains in his descendants﴾, meaning in his offspring. So there will always be among them someone who affirms the oneness of God and calls to His oneness.

﴿so that they may return﴾: perhaps those among them who associated partners with God will return through the supplication of those among them who affirmed His oneness. The expression of hope (al-tarajji, "perhaps") is attributed to Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 29:

﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, who are of the lineage (ʿaqib) of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, (p-271) with prolongation of life and blessing. So they were deceived by the respite, and they became preoccupied with luxury, the pursuit of desires, and obedience to Satan, away from the word of Tawhid (monotheism),

﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, the Qur'an,

﴿and a Messenger﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ),

﴿clear﴾, clear in his message, with the clear signs he brought.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 30:

﴿When the truth came to them﴾, [i.e.] the Qur'an,

﴿they said, "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾

"And they said," [in it: arguing arbitrarily with falsehood,]

"Why was this Qur'an not sent down" [in it: a display of contempt for it,]

"upon a man of importance from the two towns?" That is: a great man from one of the two towns, like His saying: "From them emerge the pearl and the coral" [al-Rahman: 22], meaning from one of them. The two towns are Makkah and al-Ta'if. By "the great man of Makkah" they meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and by "the great man of al-Ta'if" they meant Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. By "the great" they meant whoever had wealth and standing, and they did not realize that the great one is the one who is great in the sight of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 32:

﴿Is it they who would apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ That is, prophethood. The interrogative particle (hamza) here is for disavowal that stands on its own, rebuking them for their ignorance and expressing wonder at their presumption in choosing who is fit for prophethood.

﴿It is We who apportion among them their livelihood﴾, that by which they live, which is their sustenance,

﴿in the life of this world﴾. That is, We have not left the apportioning of the lesser thing to them, which is provision; so how would prophethood be (left to them)? Or: just as I have preferred some over others in provision, so too I single out for prophethood whomever I will.

﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees﴾. That is, We made some strong, wealthy and masters, and others weak, poor and servants,

﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾, so that some may employ others for their needs, and make them work at their trades, and put them to their tasks, until they make a living and reach their benefits: this one with his wealth, and that one with his labour.

﴿But the mercy of your Lord﴾. That is, prophethood, or the religion of God and what follows from it of success in the final return,

﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾, than what these people gather of the wreckage of the world. Having diminished the matter of this world and belittled it, he followed it with what establishes how little the world is in His sight, and so said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 33:

﴿And had it not been that mankind would be one community﴾, and had it not been the case that He disliked that they would gather in disbelief and unite upon it,

﴿We would have made﴾, because of the worthlessness of this world in Our sight,

﴿for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, ceilings of silver for their houses and stairways of silver upon which they would ascend﴾.

﴿And for their houses, doors and couches on which they recline,﴾ ﴿and adornments.﴾ That is: We would have made for the disbelievers roofs, staircases, doors and couches, all of them of silver, and We would have made for them adornment, meaning ornament of every kind. Al-zukhruf means gold, and also adornment. It is possible that the original reading was "suqufan min fiddatin wa zukhrufin", meaning that some of them were of silver and some of gold. So "saqfan" (roofs) is in the accusative by coordination with the position of "min fiddatin", and "li-buyutihim" (for their houses) is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion) from "li-man yakfuru" (for those who disbelieve). "Saqfan" is in the singular with a collective sense. Makki, Abu 'Amr and Yazid read it this way. "Al-ma'arij" is the plural of "mi'raj", which means staircases leading up to the upper floors. "'Alayha yazharun" means: they ascend upon the staircases to the roofs, that is, they climb over them.

﴿And all of that is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world.﴾ "In" is a negative particle, and "lamma" has the meaning of "illa" (except). That is: all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. It has also been read this way. Ghayr 'Asim and Hamza read "lama", on the basis that the *lam* is the distinguishing letter (al-lam al-fariqa) between the light "in" (the mukhaffafa) and the negative "in", and "ma" is a redundant particle (silah). That is: indeed all of that is the enjoyment of the life of this world.

﴿And the Hereafter﴾, that is, the reward of the Hereafter,

﴿with your Lord is for the God-fearing,﴾ for those who guard themselves against shirk.

﴿And for their houses, doors and couches on which they recline,﴾ ﴿and adornments.﴾ That is: We would have made for the disbelievers roofs, staircases, doors and couches, all of them of silver, and We would have made for them adornment, meaning ornament of every kind. Al-zukhruf means gold, and also adornment. It is possible that the original reading was "suqufan min fiddatin wa zukhrufin", meaning that some of them were of silver and some of gold. So "saqfan" (roofs) is in the accusative by coordination with the position of "min fiddatin", and "li-buyutihim" (for their houses) is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion) from "li-man yakfuru" (for those who disbelieve). "Saqfan" is in the singular with a collective sense. Makki, Abu 'Amr and Yazid read it this way. "Al-ma'arij" is the plural of "mi'raj", which means staircases leading up to the upper floors. "'Alayha yazharun" means: they ascend upon the staircases to the roofs, that is, they climb over them.

﴿And all of that is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world.﴾ "In" is a negative particle, and "lamma" has the meaning of "illa" (except). That is: all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. It has also been read this way. Ghayr 'Asim and Hamza read "lama", on the basis that the *lam* is the distinguishing letter (al-lam al-fariqa) between the light "in" (the mukhaffafa) and the negative "in", and "ma" is a redundant particle (silah). That is: indeed all of that is the enjoyment of the life of this world.

﴿And the Hereafter﴾, that is, the reward of the Hereafter,

﴿with your Lord is for the God-fearing,﴾ for those who guard themselves against shirk.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 36:

﴿And whoever turns away﴾. It is also read "wa-man ya'sha" (with fatha). The difference between the two is that when a calamity befalls his sight, it is said: "ʿashiya, yaʿshā" (he became blind in the eyes, with a weakness of sight), whereas if he looks with the look of one who has weak sight but has no affliction in him, it is said: "ʿashā, yaʿshū" (his sight grew weak at dusk). The meaning of the reading with fatha is: "and whoever goes blind" (wa-man yaʿma).

﴿from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, which is the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿deaf, dumb, and blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18]. The meaning of the reading with ḍamma is: "and whoever feigns blindness to its remembrance" (wa-man yataʿāma ʿan dhikrihi), i.e., he knows that it is the truth, yet he pretends ignorance, as in His saying: ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. ﴿We appoint for him a devil, and he becomes his companion﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "We empower him over him, so he is with him in this world and the Hereafter, driving him to sins." And in this there is an indication that whoever persists in remembrance of the Most Merciful, Satan does not become his companion.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 37:**

﴿And indeed they﴾, that is, the devils,

﴿will surely bar them﴾, that is, they prevent those who turn away (al-ʿashin),

﴿from the path﴾, from the path of guidance,

﴿while they think﴾, that is, those who turn away (al-ʿashun),

﴿that they are guided﴾. And he used the plural pronoun for "man" (man) and for the devil together, because "man" (man) is indefinite in regard to the category of the one who turns away, and a devil has been assigned to him who is likewise indefinite in his category, so it is permissible for the pronoun to refer to both of them in the plural.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾ is read in the singular according to the Iraqi readers other than Abu Bakr. That is, al-ʿāshī (the one who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful). ﴿جاءانا﴾ (*jāʾānā*, "they both came") is read in the dual by the others, meaning al-ʿāshī and his companion.

﴿He says﴾ to his devil,

﴿"O, would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!"﴾ He means the east and the west, but the term for the east was given precedence (*taghlīb*, the use of one of two terms to stand for both), as it is said: al-ʿUmarān (Abu Bakr and ʿUmar) and al-Qamarān (the sun and the moon). The intended meaning is the distance between the east and the west, and the west and the east.

﴿"Evil is the companion"﴾, you are.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 39:

﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have done wrong﴾: "since" (*idh*) here means that your wrongdoing has been established, i.e., your disbelief (*kufr*), and it has become clear, and neither you nor anyone else has any doubt that you were wrongdoers. The word *idh* is a *badal* (substitute, a term for an appositional element that replaces the preceding word) for *al-yawm* ("today").

﴿that you, in the punishment, will be sharing﴾: *annakum* ("that you") is in the nominative position, as the grammatical subject (*al-fa'iliyya*, the grammatical function of the doer of the verb). The meaning is: your sharing in the punishment will not benefit you, or the fact that you are sharing in the punishment will not benefit you. Just as the generality of an affliction would console the heart in the world, as in the words of al-Khansa':

*"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.*
*Yet none weep like my brother, but I console myself for him with consolation."*

As for these people, their sharing in the punishment does not console them, nor does it relieve them, because of the magnitude of what they are in.

It was also said: the subject is implied, meaning: this wish or this excuse will not benefit you, because you are sharing in the punishment, due to your sharing in its cause, which is disbelief. This is supported by the *qira'a* (canonical recitation) of those who read it with a *kasra* (*innakum*, with the vowel *i* on the *nun*).

(p-274) ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ That is: those who have lost the hearing of acceptance,

﴿or guide the blind?﴾ That is: those who have lost insight,

﴿and those who are in clear error﴾, and those whom God knows will die in error.

﴿فَإمّا﴾: the "ما" (ma) has been added to "إن" (in), for emphasis of the condition (tawkid lil-shart, "emphasis of the conditional"). The same applies to the heavy nun in ﴿نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ﴾, meaning: "We will surely take you away [i.e., cause you to die] before We grant you victory over them, and We will heal the hearts of the believers from them."

﴿فَإنّا مِنهم مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾: "then indeed We will take vengeance upon them," the most severe vengeance, in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 42:

﴿Or We shall show you that which We have promised them,﴾ before We take you (in death), meaning on the Day of Badr,

﴿for indeed We are over them omnipotent.﴾ Capable. He described them with their severe obstinacy in disbelief and misguidance, by His saying: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 40], and so on, then He threatened them with the punishment of this world and the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away,﴾ the two verses.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 43:

﴿So hold fast﴾, i.e., cling firmly,

﴿to that which has been revealed to you﴾, which is the Qur'an, and act upon it,

﴿indeed you are upon a straight path﴾, i.e., upon the religion that has no crookedness in it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 45:

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ The asking of the messengers is not meant as actual questioning; rather it is a metaphor (majaz) for examining (nazar) their religions and investigating (fahs) their creeds (milal): has the worship of idols ever appeared in any creed of the prophets? His examination and inquiry are sufficient in the Book of God, the inimitable (al-mu'jiz) that confirms what came before it, and in God's report in it that they ﴿worship besides God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Hajj: 71]. This verse in itself is sufficient, and there is no need for anything else.

It is also said that the Prophet ﷺ was gathered with the prophets on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), and he led them in prayer, and it was said to him: "Ask them," but he was not in doubt and did not ask. It is also said that its meaning is: "Ask the nations of those We sent, and they are the People of the Two Scriptures, namely the Torah and the Gospel; they only inform him about the books of the messengers, so when he asks them, it is as if he asked the prophets." The purpose of this question is to rebuke the idol-worshippers, showing that they are upon falsehood.

"And ask" (wa-sal), without a hamza, is read by Makki and Ali. "Rusulina" (plural of messengers) is read by Abu 'Amr. Then He consoled His Messenger ﷺ with His saying:

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "Indeed I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ What they answered him when he said, ﴿Indeed I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ is omitted, indicated by his saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 47:

﴿So when he came to them with Our signs﴾, that is, their demanding of him that he bring forth the proof for his claim and produce the sign,

﴿behold, they laughed at them﴾, they mocked them, scoffed at them, and called them magic. "Idha" (إذا) here is for suddenness (lil-mufajaah, the particle of sudden surprise), and it is the response (jawab) of "falamma" (فلما), because the verb of suddenness (fi'l al-mufajaah) with it is implied (muqaddar), and it is the governing element of the accusative (amil al-nasb) in the position (mahall) of "idha." It is as if it were said: "So when he came to them with Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 48:

﴿And We did not show them any sign except that it was greater than its sister﴾, its counterpart and companion that came before it in breaking the habitual order. The apparent wording indicates that the later sign is greater than the earlier one, but this is not so. Rather, what is meant by this statement is that they are all described as being great, and they do not differ much in this respect. This is also how people speak: "They are two brothers, each one of whom is more generous than the other."

﴿And We seized them with the punishment﴾, which is what He (exalted be He) referred to in: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], and ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ [al-A'raf: 133], and the verse.

﴿That they might return﴾, from disbelief to belief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 49:

﴿And they said, "O sorcerer!"﴾ They used to call the learned and skilled scholar "sorcerer" (sāḥir), out of their esteem for his knowledge of sorcery (siḥr),

﴿Yā ayyuhā al-sāḥir﴾ with the ḍamma on the hā' and without an alif, is the reading of [Ibn ‘Āmir and] the Syrians (Shāmī). Its basis (wajhuhu) is that the hā' was originally fatḥa because it came before the alif. When the alif fell away due to the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn), its vowel was made to follow the vowel of what preceded it (utbi‘at ḥarakatuhā ḥarakata mā qablahā).

﴿Pray for us to your Lord by what He has covenanted with you﴾, meaning: by His covenant with you, that your supplication is answered; or by His covenant with you, which is prophethood; or by what He has covenanted with you of removing the punishment from those who are guided,

﴿Indeed we are guided﴾, meaning: we are believers in it (him).
﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.﴾ They break the covenant of faith and do not keep it.

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed﴾: he himself summoned the dignitaries of the Copts, or he ordered a herald, and the herald proclaimed. This is like your saying, "The emir cut off the thief," when he ordered his amputation.

﴿among his people﴾: he made them the place of his proclamation and its target.

﴿He said: "O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers﴾, that is, the rivers of the Nile, the principal ones of which are four,

﴿flowing beneath me﴾: beneath my palace. It is also said: before me, in my gardens. The waw (و) is conjunctive, coordinating "al-anhar" (the rivers) with "mulk Misr" (the dominion of Egypt). "Tajri" (flowing) is in the accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal) describing them. Alternatively, the waw is a waw of circumstance (hal), the demonstrative is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), "al-anhar" is an attribute (sifah) of the demonstrative, and "tajri" is the predicate (khabar) of the subject.

It is reported from al-Rashid that when he read this verse he said, "I shall appoint to it the basest of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who had been his servant attending to his ablution. It is also reported from Abdullah ibn Tahir that when he was appointed over it and went out to it, as he approached it he said, "Is this the town over which Pharaoh boasted, to the point of saying, 'Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?' By God, it is less in my estimation than that I should enter it," and he turned his reins back.

﴿Do you not then see?﴾: my power and the weakness of Moses, my wealth and his poverty?!

"Am I not better than this one who is contemptible, and who can hardly express himself?"

Note: the Arabic text here reads as follows in full:

(Am) "Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. It is as if he said: "Has it been established and settled among you that I am better, and this is my condition?"

﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible﴾, weak, insignificant,

﴿and who can hardly express himself﴾, i.e., speech, because of the impediment (ratta) he had.

**﴿So why then﴾**, i.e., "why then" (فَهَلّا, *fahallā*, "why not").

**﴿were bracelets of gold cast upon him﴾**: Ḥafṣ, Yaʿqūb and Sahl read *asworatun* (أسْوِرَةٌ), the plural of *siwār* (سِوارٌ, "bracelet"). Others read *asāwiratun* (أساوِرَةٌ), the plural of *iswār* (إسْوارٌ), which is the same as *siwār*. In this form the *yāʾ* of *asāwīr* has been dropped and the *tāʾ* (ة) substituted for it.

**﴿of gold﴾**: By casting bracelets upon him he meant casting upon him the keys of kingship (مَقالِيدِ المُلْكِ), because when they wanted to make a man a ruler (تَسْوِيدَ الرَجُلِ), they would put a bracelet (سِوار) on him and put a collar (طَوْق) of gold around his neck.

**﴿or the angels came with him in procession﴾**: they walk with him, some of them accompanying others, so that they would be his supporters (أعَضادَهُ), his helpers (وأنْصارَهُ), and his aides (وأعْوانَهُ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 54:

﴿So he made his people feeble-minded﴾: he provoked them with words, led them astray, and made his speech take effect among them. It was said: he sought from them *al-khiffah* (lightness, i.e., quick compliance) and obedience, and *al-khiffah* is hastening (*al-isra'*).

﴿So they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiant people﴾, going outside the religion of Allah.

﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance on them and drowned them all.﴾ "Ā-safūnā" is derived from "asifa asafan", meaning his anger intensified. Its meaning is that they went to excess in acts of disobedience, so they deserved that Our punishment and Our vengeance be hastened upon them, and that We not show forbearance toward them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 56:

﴿So We made them a precedent﴾: the plural of "sālif" (one who has passed on), like "khādim" (servant) and "khadam" (servants). It is also read "sulufan" (in a plural pattern), and Ḥamzah and ʿAlī read it as the plural of "salīf," meaning: a group that has passed on.

﴿and an example﴾: and a matter of remarkable import, going on like a proverb, by which proverbs are coined. It is said: "Your case is like the case of the people of Pharaoh."

﴿for the later ones﴾: for those who come after them. Its meaning is: We made them an exemplar for the later ones among the disbelievers, who take them as a model in deserving the like of their punishment and its descending upon them, because they commit the like of their deeds, and an example that they relate.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 43, verse 57:**

﴿When the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾. It was narrated: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to Quraysh (p-278) ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ (21:98), they became angry. Ibn al-Za'bara (Ibn al-Zib'ara) said: 'O Muhammad, is this specific to us and our gods, or is it for all nations?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is for you, your gods, and all nations.' He said: 'Do you not claim that Jesus, son of Mary, is a prophet, and you praise him and his mother highly? You know that the Christians worship them both, that 'Uzayr is worshipped, and that the angels are worshipped. If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them.' They rejoiced and laughed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) fell silent. Then Allah (Exalted) revealed ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us will be kept far from it﴾ (21:101)." This verse was revealed. The meaning: when Ibn al-Za'bara cited Jesus, son of Mary, as an example for their gods, and disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through the worship of Jesus by the Christians,

﴿your people﴾, meaning Quraysh,

﴿because of it﴾, because of this example,

﴿turn away﴾: a clamour and uproar rose up from them out of joy and laughter at what they heard of the Prophet's (ﷺ) silencing by his argument. The reading "yaṣuddūn" (with a ḍammah on the ṣād) is that of Madani, Shami, al-A'sha and Ali; it derives from "al-ṣudūd" (aversion), meaning: because of this example they turn away from the truth and avoid it. It has also been said that it derives from "al-ṣadīd" (al-ṣadīd, a clamour), and both are dialectal forms, like "ya'kifu" and "ya'kuf" (both meaning "to remain devoted to").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 58:

﴿And they said: "Are our gods better, or is he?"﴾ They mean: our gods, in your view, are not inferior to Jesus. If Jesus is among the fuel of the Fire, then the matter of our gods is even lighter.

﴿They did not strike this parable﴾, that is, they did not coin this example

﴿for you except for disputation﴾, only for the sake of argument and winning in speech, not seeking to distinguish truth from falsehood.

﴿Rather, they are a people given to contention﴾, stubborn, fierce in opposition. Their habit is *lijaj* (obstinate quarrelling). The reason is that His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98] was intended only for the idols, because *ma* (the Arabic relative pronoun "ما") is used for non-rational beings. However, Ibn al-Zib'ara, through his deception, when he saw that the wording of God's speech could bear the sense of generality (*al-'umum*), while knowing that its intended referent was only their idols and nothing else, found room for the stratagem. He turned the wording toward inclusiveness and encompassment of every object of worship other than God, through the way of obstinacy, argumentation, love of overpowering, and arrogant defiance. He was shameless in this, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was distressed until his Lord answered him.

(p-279) ﴿Hu﴾ (He is) — that is, Jesus — ﴿only a servant﴾, like all the other servants, ﴿upon whom We bestowed favour﴾ with prophethood, ﴿and We made him an example for the Children of Israel﴾, that is, We made him a wondrous lesson, like the proverb that circulates among the Children of Israel.

"And if We willed, We would have made from among you angels in the earth [who would] succeed [you]." That is: in place of you. So said al-Zajjaj. In "Jami' al-Ulum" it says: "We would have made in your place," and "min" here carries the meaning of "in place of."

﴿Yakhlifun﴾: they would succeed you in the earth, or the angels would succeed one another. It was also said: "If We willed," by Our power over wondrous matters, "We would have made from among you," O men, "angels" who would succeed you in the earth, just as your children succeed you. Just as We brought forth Jesus from a female without a male, so that you would recognize Our distinction through overwhelming power, and so that you would know that the angels are bodies that are produced only from bodies, while the Eternal is exalted above that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 61:

﴿And indeed, it is a sign (ʿilm) for the Hour﴾. That is, ʿĪsā is among the things by which the coming of the Hour is known. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) recited: "la-ʿalamun lil-sāʿah", where ʿalam means ʿalāmah (sign). The meaning is: his descent is a sign for the Hour.

﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾: fa-lā tamtarunna bihā, meaning fa-lā tashukkunna fīhā, from al-mirya (ṭ-mirya, doubt), which is al-shakk (doubt).

﴿And follow Me﴾: it is read with the yāʾ in both places (wa-ittabiʿūnī) by Sahl and Yaʿqūb. That is: follow my guidance and my law, or my messenger. Or it is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to say it.

﴿This is a straight path﴾: that is, this is what I am calling you to.

And let not Satan avert you (from belief in the Hour, or from following), [Qur'an 43:62 — "And let not Satan avert you. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy."]

Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy, evidently hostile, since he expelled your father from the Garden, stripping him of his garment of light.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 63:**

﴿When ʿĪsā came with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the miracles, or with the verses of the Injil (Gospel), and the clear and evident laws,

﴿he said: "I have come to you with wisdom"﴾, that is, with the Injil and the laws,

﴿and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾, and that is the matter of religion, not the matter of worldly affairs,

﴿so fear Allah and obey me.﴾
(p-280) ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾ This is the complete end of the speech of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him).

﴿Then the factions differed﴾: the sects that split into parties after Jesus, namely the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites), the Nestoriyya (Nestorians), the Malkaniyya (Melkites), and the Sham'uniyya (Shamʿūniyya),

﴿from among them﴾: from among the Christians,

﴿so woe to those who did wrong﴾: because of what they said about Jesus, which was disbelief in him,

﴿from the punishment of a painful day﴾: and that is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 43, verse 66:

﴿Do they await anything but the Hour?﴾ The pronoun (*al-ḍamīr*) refers either to the people of ʿIsa (Jesus), or to the disbelievers.

﴿That it come upon them﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, an appositional noun that replaces the preceding noun) for "*al-sāʿa*" (the Hour). That is, "Do they await anything but the coming of the Hour?"

﴿Suddenly while they perceive not﴾ means: while they are heedless, because they are occupied with the affairs of their worldly life. This is like His saying: ﴿They will be seized while they are disputing﴾ [Yasin: 49].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 67:

﴿Al-akhilla'﴾ (the close friends), the plural of "khalil" (intimate friend),

﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day), i.e., the Day of Resurrection,

﴿Ba'DuHum li-ba'Din 'aduwwun illa al-muttaqin﴾ (some of them will be enemies to others, except the God-fearing), i.e., the believers. The accusative of "yawma'idhin" is governed by "'aduwwun" (enemy), meaning: on that Day every friendship between those who befriend one another for other than the sake of God will be severed and will turn into enmity and hatred, except the friendship of those who befriend one another for the sake of God, for that is the friendship that remains.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 68:

"Yā ʿibādī" (O My servants), with the yā' pronounced in both continuous recitation and pause, is read by Madani, Shami and Abu ʿAmr; with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥah, by Abu Bakr; and the rest read it with the yā' elided.

﴿No fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾. This is a report of what the God-fearing, who love one another for the sake of God, will be called with on that Day.

"Those who" (alladhina) is in the accusative position, an adjective (sifah) describing "My servants," because the latter is a vocative construction with an attached noun (munada mudaf).

"Who believed in Our signs" (amanu bi-ayatina): they affirmed Our signs as true.

"And were Muslims" (wa-kanu muslimin): submitting to Allah, yielding to Him.

Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, honoured (Quran 43:70). [Note: the text is translated below in full as requested.]

Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, [the believing women of the world]. You will be made to rejoice (tuhbarun) with a joy whose radiance (hibar) — that is, its trace — appears upon your faces.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 71:

﴿They will be served with platters of gold﴾, plural of "ṣaḥfah" (platter),

﴿and cups﴾, meaning: also of gold. The "kūb" is a jug without a handle (ʿurwah),

﴿and therein﴾, that is, in Paradise,

﴿is whatever the souls desire﴾. The reading of Madani, Shami and Hafs is with the pronoun (hāʾ) returning to the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) retained, while others omit it because of the length of the relative clause with the verb, the subject and the object,

﴿and delightful to the eyes﴾. This is a comprehensive enumeration of the types of blessings, for they are either things desired by the hearts, or things delightful to the eyes,

﴿and you therein will abide forever﴾.

This is the Arabic commentary text; I'll translate it faithfully.

﴿And that is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit, for what you used to do.﴾ "That" (تِلْكَ) is a demonstrative referring to the Paradise mentioned, and it is the subject (mubtada'); "the Paradise" (al-jannah) is the predicate (khabar), and "which you have been made to inherit" (allati ooritumuha) is a qualifying clause (sifah) of "the Paradise." Alternatively, "the Paradise" is a qualifier (sifah) of the subject, which is the demonstrative, and "which you have been made to inherit" is the predicate of the subject. Or "which you have been made to inherit" is the qualifier of the subject. "For what you used to do" (bima kuntum ta'maluna) is the predicate, and the preposition "bi" (the ba') is linked to an omitted element, meaning "obtained" (hasilah) or "existing" (ka'inah), as in the adverbial phrases that occur as predicates. In the first case, it is linked to "you have been made to inherit" (ooritumuha), and [the Paradise] is likened, in its remaining with its people, to an inheritance that remains with the heirs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 73:

﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you eat.﴾ "Min" (مِن) is for partitive (lil-tab'id) meaning: you eat only some of it, and its remnants remain on its trees, so it is adorned with fruit forever. And in a hadith: "No man plucks from its fruit in Paradise except that two of the same kind grow in its place."

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ The phrase "خَبَرٌ بَعْدَ خَبَرٍ" (khabar ba'da khabar) means that "خالدون" (khalidun, "abiding forever") is a second predicate (khabar) following the first predicate of "إنّ" (inna), with "في عذاب جهنم" (in the punishment of Hell) being the first.

﴿Lā yufattaru ʿanhum﴾ (they will not be relieved of it): another predicate; that is, it will not be lightened, nor will it be reduced.

﴿wa-hum fīhi﴾ (and they will be in it): in the punishment.

﴿mublisūn﴾ (despairing): hopeless of relief, bewildered.

"And We did not wrong them," by the punishment,

"but they themselves were the wrongdoers." "Hum" (the pronoun "they themselves") is a separating pronoun (fasl), which serves to emphasize the subject and to confine the predicate to it.

﴿And they will call out, "O Malik!"﴾ When they despaired of the abatement of the punishment, they called out, "O Malik!" — and he is the keeper of the Fire. It was related to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that Ibn Masʿud recited, "Yā Māl" (O Māl). He said, "How much the people of the Fire are preoccupied away from tarkhīm!"

﴿That your Lord may put an end to us﴾: that He may cause us to die, from "qaḍā ʿalayhi" (he decreed death upon him), when He causes him to die,

﴿So Musa struck him and put an end to him﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. The meaning is: ask your Lord to decree an end upon us.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ In the punishment, you will not be freed from it by death or by abatement.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾: this is the speech of Allah (exalted be He). The subject of "said" (qala) must be the pronoun referring to Allah, because when they asked Malik to ask Allah to decree judgment against them, Allah answered them with this. It was also said that it is connected to the speech of Malik, and what is meant by his saying "We have brought you" is the angels, since they are the messengers of Allah and he (Malik) is among them.

﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾: they do not accept it and they recoil from it, because with falsehood comes ease (al-da'a), and with truth comes hardship (al-ta'ab).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 79:

﴿Or have they determined an affair?﴾ That is, have the idolaters of Makkah firmly decided ﴿an affair﴾ concerning their scheming and plotting against Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Then indeed We are determined.﴾ That is, (We are determined in) Our scheme, just as they determined their scheme. They used to confer with one another and hold secret consultations concerning the affair of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of the Quraysh).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 80:

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret (sirrahum)﴾, meaning the discourse of their own souls (hadith anfusihim),

﴿and their private conference (najwahum)﴾, meaning what they discuss among themselves and conceal from others,

﴿Yes indeed﴾, meaning We hear both of them and are aware of them,

﴿and Our messengers﴾, i.e., the guardian angels (al-hafazah), ﴿are with them and record﴾, meaning with them, recording that.

And on the authority of Yahya ibn Mu'adh: "Whoever conceals his sins from people and reveals them to One from whom no hidden thing is concealed has made Him the least of those who look upon him, and this is one of the signs of hypocrisy (nifaq)."

(p-283) ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, and if that were established by proof,

﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾: I would be the first to revere that son, the first to submit to him and to obey him, just as a man reveres the son of a king out of reverence for his father. This statement is given on the basis of supposition, and what is intended is the negation of a son. That is because He made worship dependent on the existence of a son, and that is impossible in itself, so what was made dependent on it is likewise impossible. A parallel to this is the statement of Sa'id ibn Jubayr to al-Hajjaj, when the latter said to him, "By God, I will exchange you for the Fire that blazes (nar talaza)," [Sa'id replied]: "If I knew that this was up to you, I would not worship any god other than you."

It has also been said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of the worshippers," meaning: the first of those who affirm the oneness of God, denying your saying that a son is attributed to Him.

It has also been said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of those who are most disdainful (al-anifin) that He should have a son," deriving from "'abida ya'badu," when one's nose becomes exceedingly proud; so one is then called 'abd and 'abid. It is also read as "al-'abidin" (with a different vowelling). It has also been said that the "in" is negative, meaning: "There was not for the Most Merciful a son; so I am the first to say this, and to worship and to affirm His oneness."

It is narrated that al-Nadr said: "The angels are the daughters of God." So this verse was revealed, and al-Nadr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: 'There was not for the Most Merciful a son, so I am the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah in saying that He has no son.'" ("Walad" is read as "wuld" by Hamzah and Ali.)

Then He declared His essence free of taking a son, saying:

Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe (Qur'an 43:82). That is: He is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and the Throne. Therefore He is not a body (jism), for if He were a body He would not have been able to create them. And if He is not a body, He cannot have a child, because begetting (tawallud) is a attribute of bodies.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 83:**

﴿So leave them to plunge into their vain talk﴾, in their falsehood,

﴿and to play﴾, in their worldly life,

﴿until they encounter their Day which they are promised﴾, i.e., the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah). This is evidence that what they say is of the nature of ignorance, plunging (khawd), and play (la'ib).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 84:

﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. He included the meaning of an attribute in His name (exalted is He), and therefore the adverbial phrase was attached to it in His saying "in the heaven" and "and on the earth," just as you say: "He is Hatim in Ta'i, and Hatim in Taghlib," with the inclusion of the meaning of "al-jawad" (the generous), for which he was famous, as if you had said: "He is generous in Ta'i, generous in Taghlib." It was also read: "And He is the One who is in the heaven Allah and on the earth Allah." Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 3]. So it is as if He included the meaning of "al-ma'bud" (the one worshipped). The returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted because of the length of the speech, as in their saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you anything," and the estimated reading is: "And He is the One who He is in the heaven God," and "God" is raised as the predicate of an implied subject (mubtada' mudmar), and "God" is not raised by being the subject, and "in the heaven" is the predicate, since the relative clause would then be devoid of a returning pronoun referring to the relative pronoun.

﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, in His sayings and His deeds,

﴿the All-Knowing﴾, of what has been and what will be.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 43, verse 85:**

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning: the knowledge of its establishment (qiyamah),

﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. "يُرْجَعُونَ" (*yurja'un*, "they will be returned"), read with the *ya'* by Makki, Hamza and Ali.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 86:

﴿And they do not possess﴾, their gods,

﴿those whom they invoke﴾, i.e., they invoke them,

﴿besides Him﴾, besides Allah,

﴿intercession﴾, as they claimed, that they are their intercessors with Allah,

﴿except those who bear witness to the truth﴾, i.e., but rather whoever bears witness to the truth, with the word of Tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness),

﴿and they know﴾, that Allah is truly their Lord, and they believe that it is He who possesses intercession. This is an exception that is either disjunctive (munqati') or connected (muttasil), because among those who are invoked besides Allah are the angels.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verse 87:

﴿And if you were to ask them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾

﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ i.e., the polytheists,

﴿who created them, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ Not the idols, nor the angels.

﴿So how are they turned away?﴾ i.e., how, or from where, are they diverted from monotheism (tawhid), despite this acknowledgment?!

And His saying, "O my Lord," read in the genitive (jarr) by ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah, meaning: and [He has knowledge] of the Hour and of His saying [that is, the Prophet's saying].

﴿O my Lord﴾. The pronoun in "His saying" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), because his mention has preceded in His words: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81]. The rest of the readers read it in the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the position (maḥall) of "the Hour" — that is, He knows the Hour and He knows his saying, that is, the saying of Muhammad: "O my Lord." The words "al-qīl," "al-qawl," "al-qāl," and "al-maqāl" all have the same meaning. It is also permissible that the genitive and accusative readings be based on the assumption of an elided particle of oath (ḥarf al-qasam), with its omission, and the answer of the oath is: ﴿Indeed, these are a people who do not believe﴾, as if it were said: "And I swear by His saying: ﴿O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾." And God's swearing by His saying is an elevation of it from Him and an exaltation of his supplication and his turning to Him.

ﷻ"So turn away from them" — that is, turn away from calling them, despairing of their faith, bid them farewell, and leave them.

"And say," to them:

"Peace" — that is, a greeting of parting from you, and a severing of ties.

"But they will come to know," — a warning from Allah to them, and a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And with the letter ta' (reading "they will come to know" in the second person, i.e., "you will come to know"), it is read by the people of Medina and Syria.
